module.title: 4 · Diagnostics
module.summary: First-stage F flags weak instruments; over-identification tests probe exclusion.

stages.title: Weak instruments and the first-stage F
stages.html:
How strong is your instrument?

Relevance is not yes/no — it is a matter of degree. A weak instrument barely moves x, so Cov(z,x) is tiny and the IV ratio divides by near-zero. Consequences:

  • 2SLS standard errors balloon — estimates become wildly imprecise.
  • Worse, weak instruments reintroduce bias toward OLS in finite samples, and the usual SEs understate the true uncertainty.

The standard diagnostic is the first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instruments — from sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue. A common rule of thumb (Staiger–Stock):

first-stage F ≳ 10 → instrument is "strong enough"

Key idea. Always report the first-stage F. An F in the low single digits is a red flag: your 2SLS results may be unreliable no matter how clean the exclusion story is.

stages.title: Over-identification: a partial check on exclusion
stages.html:
When you have spare instruments

If you have more valid instruments than endogenous regressors, the model is over-identified. Each instrument gives its own estimate of β₁; if all instruments are valid, those estimates should agree (up to sampling noise). An over-identification test (Sargan / Hansen J) checks exactly this.

The intuition: take the 2SLS residuals and regress them on all the instruments. Under a valid set, the instruments should have no explanatory power for the residual, so

J = n·R² ~ χ²(#instruments − #endogenous)

A small J / large p-value is consistent with valid instruments; a small p-value says at least one instrument fails exclusion (or the model is misspecified).

Key idea. Over-ID tests can only reject validity — passing is reassuring but not proof, and the test is silent in the just-identified case (one instrument, one endogenous regressor), where there is nothing to compare against.

stages.title: Weak vs strong: F and 2SLS side by side
stages.note: Same structure, only the instrument's strength changes. Watch the first-stage F and the 2SLS estimate/SE move together.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000

def run(pi):
    u = rng.normal(0,1,n); z = rng.normal(0,1,n)
    x = pi*z + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
    y = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)   # true beta1 = 2
    F  = sm.OLS(x, sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue
    iv = IV2SLS(y, sm.add_constant(x), sm.add_constant(z)).fit()
    return F, iv.params[1], iv.bse[1]

print(f"{'pi':>5}{'first-F':>10}{'2SLS b1':>10}{'SE':>8}")
pis=[0.05,0.1,0.3,0.8,1.5]; Fs=[]; bs=[]
for pi in pis:
    F,b,se=run(pi); Fs.append(F); bs.append(b)
    tag='  <-- weak (F<10)' if F<10 else ''
    print(f'{pi:5.2f}{F:10.1f}{b:10.2f}{se:8.2f}{tag}')

fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,3.7))
ax[0].plot(pis,Fs,'o-',color='#da9100',lw=2); ax[0].axhline(10,color='#c9c6ac',ls='--')
ax[0].set_title('first-stage F'); ax[0].set_xlabel('pi')
ax[1].plot(pis,bs,'o-',color='#af983f',lw=2); ax[1].axhline(2,color='#c9c6ac',ls='--')
ax[1].set_title('2SLS beta1_hat'); ax[1].set_xlabel('pi')
fig.tight_layout()

stages.title: Weak-instrument slider
stages.note: Drag π. The title shows the first-stage F and the 2SLS estimate. Below ~10 the estimate jumps around and the SE explodes — the weak-instrument danger zone.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); n=1000
u=rng.normal(0,1,n); z=rng.normal(0,1,n)
x={{pi}}*z+1.0*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
y=1+2*x+3*u+rng.normal(0,1,n)
F=sm.OLS(x,sm.add_constant(z)).fit().fvalue
iv=IV2SLS(y,sm.add_constant(x),sm.add_constant(z)).fit()
b,se=iv.params[1],iv.bse[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar([0],[b],yerr=[1.96*se],fmt='o',color='#da9100',capsize=8,ms=10,label='2SLS 95% CI')
plt.axhline(2,color='#af983f',ls='--',lw=2,label='true=2')
plt.xlim(-1,1); plt.xticks([]); plt.legend()
weak=' WEAK' if F<10 else ' strong'
plt.title(f'F={F:.1f}{weak}   2SLS b1={b:.2f}  SE={se:.2f}')

stages.title: Over-identification (Sargan) intuition
stages.note: Two instruments, one endogenous x. We compute the Sargan J statistic by regressing 2SLS residuals on the instruments. Valid instruments → large p-value; an instrument that leaks into y → tiny p-value.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import IV2SLS
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(3); n=1000
u  = rng.normal(0,1,n)
z1 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z2 = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x  = 0.8*z1 + 0.7*z2 + 1.0*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y  = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + rng.normal(0,1,n)       # both instruments excluded -> valid

exog  = sm.add_constant(x)
instr = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z1, z2])
iv = IV2SLS(y, exog, instr).fit()
print('2SLS beta1_hat =', round(iv.params[1],3), ' (true 2)')

# Sargan J: regress 2SLS residuals on ALL instruments; J = n*R^2 ~ chi2(#instr - #endog)
resid = y - exog @ iv.params
aux = sm.OLS(resid, instr).fit()
J = n * aux.rsquared
dof = instr.shape[1] - exog.shape[1]   # 3 instrument cols - 2 exog cols = 1
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(J, dof)
print(f'Sargan J = {J:.3f}  dof={dof}  p-value = {p:.3f}')
print('large p-value -> no evidence against instrument validity (good)')

# Now BREAK exclusion: let z2 leak directly into y
y_bad = 1 + 2*x + 3*u + 1.5*z2 + rng.normal(0,1,n)
iv_b = IV2SLS(y_bad, exog, instr).fit()
resid_b = y_bad - exog @ iv_b.params
J_b = n * sm.OLS(resid_b, instr).fit().rsquared
p_b = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(J_b, dof)
print(f'\nwith z2 invalid:  J = {J_b:.2f}  p-value = {p_b:.3f}  -> test REJECTS validity')

stages.title: Check: reading the first-stage F
stages.prompt: Your first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instrument is 2.3. What is the appropriate concern?
choices: The instrument is weak; 2SLS may be biased and very imprecise
Nothing — any positive F is fine
stages.hint: Compare against the rule-of-thumb threshold of about 10.
stages.explain: An F well below 10 signals a weak instrument: the first stage barely moves x, so 2SLS estimates are imprecise and biased toward OLS, with unreliable standard errors.

stages.title: Check: the over-ID test
stages.prompt: With two instruments and one endogenous regressor, the Sargan/Hansen J test returns a very small p-value. This suggests…
choices: at least one instrument likely violates the exclusion restriction
stages.hint: The test compares the estimates implied by different instruments.
stages.explain: A small p-value rejects the null that all instruments are valid: the over-identifying instruments disagree, pointing to an exclusion violation (or misspecification). It cannot run in the just-identified case.

stages.title: First-stage F vs the rule of thumb
stages.prompt: The first stage regresses x on the excluded instrument; the F-statistic on that instrument is 6.4. Using the Staiger–Stock rule of thumb (F ≈ 10), how far above or below the threshold are you? Enter a signed number (e.g. −3.6).
stages.hint: Subtract the threshold from your F: 6.4 − 10.
stages.explain: 6.4 − 10 = −3.6, i.e. 3.6 below the rule-of-thumb 10 — a weak instrument. This is the significance≠strength trap again in numbers: that same first stage could have a significant t-stat, yet an F of 6.4 means 2SLS is biased toward OLS with distorted standard errors. 'Significant' and 'strong' are different claims; only the F speaks to strength. Boundary: F ≳ 10 is a rough threshold, not a bright line — values just above it are reassuring, low single digits are a clear red flag regardless of how clean the exclusion story is.

stages.title: What a passed over-ID test proves
stages.prompt: Your over-identified model has 3 instruments for 1 endogenous regressor. The Sargan/Hansen J test returns a large p-value (you fail to reject). What can you correctly conclude?
choices: The exclusion restriction is now proven — all 3 instruments are valid
The result is consistent with valid instruments, but exclusion remains an untested assumption
At least one instrument violates exclusion
The instruments are strong (high first-stage F)
why: The over-ID test can only reject; a non-rejection never proves validity.
That is what a SMALL p-value (rejection) would suggest, not a large one.
The J test checks exclusion/over-ID agreement, not strength — strength is the first-stage F.
stages.hint: The J test can only ever reject validity; ask what failing to reject does and doesn't establish.
stages.explain: This is the passed-test-proves-exogeneity trap. The over-ID (Sargan/Hansen J) test can only reject validity: a large p-value is consistent with valid instruments but proves nothing — the test has low power and must assume at least one instrument is valid to anchor on. Exclusion/exogeneity stays an argument you defend, not a result you read off. The strength distractor confuses two diagnostics: weakness is the first-stage F, validity is the J test. Boundary: the J test is also silent when the model is just-identified (one instrument, one regressor) — there are no spare instruments to disagree, so there is nothing to test.
